title: Chiggerville (15Oh1)
summary: In Ohio County, Chiggerville is a Late Archaic shell midden left by hunter-gatherers who gathered freshwater mussels there from roughly 3000 to 1000 BC.
bodyMarkdown:
In Ohio County lies Chiggerville, recorded as site 15Oh1. It is a Late Archaic shell midden, used roughly from 3000 to 1000 BC. The [Kentucky Heritage Council's Chiggerville page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Chiggerville.aspx) describes a deposit measuring 170 by 350 feet and more than 4 feet thick.

## Living beside a mussel bed

Like many Archaic shell middens in Kentucky, Chiggerville grew up where mussels were plentiful. Native hunter-gatherers returned to it as part of their seasonal rounds, gathering freshwater mussels in large numbers. The discarded shells, along with ash, bone and tools, built up the midden over many generations.

The thick deposit and the large number of stone tools point to a change that began in the late Middle Archaic. People were moving around less and staying longer in places rich in food. Most spear points from Chiggerville belong to the Saratoga Cluster, unlike the Raddatz points that dominate at the earlier Baker site.

## What people ate

The site shows a varied diet. People caught freshwater drum, catfish and softshell turtles with bone fishhooks on plant-fiber lines. They trapped and netted snapping turtles and mud turtles.

They also gathered plants. Acorns and hickory nuts were favorites, along with blackberry, grape, strawberry and persimmon, and the seeds of knotweed and goosefoot. The state page suggests that nuts and seeds were stored for winter.

## Excavations and burials

The University of Kentucky excavated Chiggerville in 1938 and again in 2009. The work recovered several thousand artifacts and documented 114 human burials, 17 dog burials, and many hearths, cooking pits and trash pits.

The 1938 dig came during a wider Depression-era push on these sites. A Kentucky Archaeological Survey booklet on Archaic shell middens explains that Works Progress Administration crews, directed by University of Kentucky professor William S. Webb, excavated several Archaic shell middens between 1937 and 1941. These excavations recovered thousands of burials of both people and dogs, and they remain central to the study of Archaic life in the Southeast.

## Hunters and bannerstones

Archaic hunters threw spears with an atlatl, or spearthrower, often weighted with a drilled stone called a bannerstone. Some made these with great care. Hunters at these middens favored a humped style, while hunters in south-central Indiana preferred a double-notched butterfly shape. The style may have signaled where a hunter came from.

A finely made bannerstone may also have marked skill or leadership within a kin group.

Chiggerville is part of a larger Archaic world that includes Indian Knoll.

## Kentucky today

Chiggerville is a protected archaeological site, and the state does not share its location. Collections from these shell middens are curated at the William S. Webb Museum of Anthropology at the University of Kentucky. Researchers still study them for what they show about the health and lives of ancient hunter-gatherers.
